analysis.one_liner: Lets patients sue their employer-sponsored health insurer in state court for malpractice and wrongful death.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors in 1997, was referred to the Senate labor committee and never received a hearing, vote, or action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under a 1974 federal law called ERISA, employers' health plans are shielded from most state lawsuits. When an employer-sponsored insurer makes a coverage or treatment decision that injures a patient, the patient often cannot sue the insurer for malpractice or wrongful death in state court — courts have split on this, and in many states the door is closed. This bill would change ERISA so those state lawsuits are allowed. It never got past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients covered by employer-sponsored health plans who are harmed by an insurer's treatment or coverage decisions, and their families, who would gain the right to seek malpractice, personal injury, or wrongful death damages from the insurer in state court [S2][S3]. Patients would also benefit because insurers facing liability have an added reason not to restrict care — the bill itself cites evidence that coverage determinations affect the health care patients actually receive [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Adds an exception to ERISA's preemption rules so state-law claims for medical malpractice, personal injury, or wrongful death against entities providing insurance or administrative services to employee health plans are not blocked [S2][S3].

Restores accountability of employer-sponsored health insurers for the health effects of their treatment rules and coverage decisions, and gives patients legal redress when those decisions cause harm — the stated purposes of the bill [S3].

Would resolve an acknowledged split among federal appeals courts over whether ERISA preempts malpractice suits against employer-sponsored health insurers, ending a situation where injured patients in some jurisdictions have no right to sue at all [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employer-sponsored health insurers and the companies that provide insurance or administrative services to employee health plans would face exposure to state-court malpractice, personal injury, and wrongful death damages, and employers and insurers would likely see higher premiums or administrative costs [S2][S3]. Some of that cost could be passed to employers and workers as higher plan costs [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employee benefit plans

drawbacks.text: Opening insurers to state-court damages could raise the cost of employer-sponsored health coverage, costs that employers and workers sharing premiums would ultimately bear [S2][S3].

The bill removes a uniform federal shield but leaves courts to sort out a contested area of law — Congress itself found the courts of appeals are split on whether ERISA preempts these suits, so the boundary of the new right would be litigated case by case [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a meaningful one: patients injured by an insurer's coverage decision currently have, in several jurisdictions, no way to recover damages at all, because the federal shield applies to the insurer while malpractice claims can only run against doctors who did not make the decision [S3]. The cost is higher litigation exposure for insurers and potentially higher premiums, and the practical reach of the new right would depend on how courts apply it. On balance it is a targeted fix to a real gap in accountability, though it would add cost and legal uncertainty to employer-based coverage.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the bill on July 31, 1997 and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S5][S3].
No further action was ever taken: the bill never had a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote [S5].
Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and bills not reported out of committee expire with it [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employer-sponsored health insurers and the companies that administer employee health plans are better off, because they kept ERISA's shield against state malpractice and wrongful death suits, which the bill would have removed. Injured patients remain unable to sue in the jurisdictions where courts have held the shield applies [S3][S5].

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it; it was referred to committee and never advanced [S5][S3].

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and died in committee without a vote, so no roll calls or bipartisan coalition ever formed around it [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill's sole substantive effect is to strip ERISA preemption so these insurers can be sued for malpractice, personal injury, and wrongful death arising from their coverage and treatment decisions — a shield the bill's findings say has left injured patients without redress [S3]. The industry's interest in keeping that shield runs directly against patients' right to recover.

industries.industry: Employee benefits administration and third-party administration firms
industries.note: The bill extends liability to any entity providing insurance or administrative services to an employee health plan, not just the insurer itself, so plan administrators would also face state-court damages claims [S3].

Employers would likely face higher premiums or administrative costs from insurer litigation exposure, though the bill does not impose liability on employers as plan sponsors beyond the entities providing insurance or administrative services [S2][S3].
